g.text: C218 · Light sources: the missing on-chip laser

text.style: font-size: 9.5px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #a1a1a6

g.text: Book Sec. 1.4.4 · silicon cannot (yet) make its own light on the chip — so where does the light come from?

text.style: font-weight: 700; font-size: 11px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #f6f6f6

g.text: 1 · The problem: no light source on the chip

text.style: font-size: 9px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #64d2ff

g.text: every chip in production borrows light from an external laser

g.text: Edge and grating couplers have become more efficient — but without

g.text: an on-chip source, the applications of these chips stay limited.

g.text: ✗ III-V does not fit the standard CMOS process

g.text: ✗ bonding: high cost, low yield ✗ available III-V wafers are small

g.text: 3 · Candidate: germanium (Ge) as the gain medium

text.style: font-size: 9px; font-family: 'Inter', 'DejaVu Sans'; text-anchor: start; fill: #30d158

g.text: CMOS-compatible — but its band gap is indirect, so it emits light poorly
